name: Beth Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a line crew for the electricity company and still take the awkward repairs myself. My two-year technical diploma taught me circuits, but I learned to teach apprentices by putting a meter in their hands and making them explain the reading. I use an AI tool now and then to turn rough notes into a tidy handover, after I have checked the line. My husband Ivo and I have grown children, about three months of expenses saved and no settled date for retirement. My pay is ordinary for linework, and there are some other utilities within reach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues that a faster handover is useful if the apprentice can still find the switch number and test result. A good repair should be easy to explain to the next crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This mild change would leave my own shifts and wages alone. Three months saved gives Ivo and me breathing room, though we still need to work before choosing a retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading repairs and continue checking occasional AI handovers against the meter sheet. In the first year I would ask an apprentice to read one report aloud and point to the actual test result.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I would not change our household plan for a shorter form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why have the apprentice read it aloud?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A missing test result sounds obvious when someone has to explain the line condition. I would rather catch a missing power-line test result at the depot than during the next callout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn a new AI tool for this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for a small change. I already use one sometimes, and I would keep the same checks unless another tool proved clearer.

say: **AI handovers** help when switch numbers and meter results stay visible.
**Clear explanations** help the next line crew work safely.
think: My **shifts and wages** remain secure in the plateau.
Three months saved gives **breathing room**, though retirement still needs work income.
do: **Keep** leading repairs and checking occasional AI handovers.
**Ask** an apprentice to read a report aloud and locate the test result.
feel: **Calm** about work and the household plan.
S0.quote: I would rather catch a missing power-line test result at the depot than during the next callout.
fieldNote: She uses **AI occasionally** for handovers, without seeking a new skill in this mild picture.
Her **three-month cushion** supports calm but does not yet settle retirement affordability.

steps.text: Keep leading repairs and checking occasional AI handovers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the call desk and ordering change first, while field robots come more slowly. A planned route should earn our trust on a real truck run before it is used to set a repair time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tool could save us a wasted drive, and I would welcome that. I do worry that apprentices could get a tight schedule with nobody left in dispatch to tell them about access, though I expect my own pay to hold for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would run the new route plan beside our old directions for six mixed fault calls. During the first year I would show the dispatch supervisor the wrong turns and the saved minutes, then use it on the routes where it proves accurate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for the younger crew, but comfortable enough to test a useful idea. Our household would not need to cut spending in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which wrong turn worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The service lane behind the workshop has a height bar our bucket truck cannot clear. I would record the detour and whether the plan learned the truck route next time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the tool saves time on five of six calls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use it for the five routes that worked and keep a manual note for the sixth. A field trial should change what a line crew does, not just decorate a report.

say: **Desk automation** arrives before physical line robots.
**Truck trials** should decide whether a route plan sets repair times.
think: A **useful route** could save a drive.
My **own pay** looks secure, but apprentices may inherit missing dispatch details.
do: **Compare** AI route plans with old directions for six faults.
**Use** proven routes and keep manual notes for the access failure.
feel: **Uneasy** for apprentices, while household income stays secure.
S1.quote: A field trial should change what a line crew does, not just decorate a report.
fieldNote: Her **steady adaptability** shows in partial adoption after a six-call trial.
She expects **her pay** to hold, so concern focuses on apprentices and access details.

steps.text: Test AI routes against six mixed fault calls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AI by 2028 changes dispatch first, while capable line repair robots arrive about 2031. The three years between should be used for real hands-on trials, not promises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be near sixty-three when robots reach field work, and I expected several more years of earning if my health holds. Three months saved will not bridge a long loss of repair shifts, and some nearby employers may be buying the same machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask to practise the robot stop control on de-energised equipment if the company offers paid time. In the first year after 2028 I would use that control in supervised trials and ask nearby utilities about actual senior repair vacancies; if robots cut my shifts after 2031, I would apply for a posted job that covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can learn a robot stop control, but I cannot make a second utility keep every lineworker on its rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you practise in the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would deliberately give the robot a wrong isolation reading and stop it before it touches the line. The crew should see the failed attempt in the record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children help if work fell away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ivo and I would speak to our children about what is happening, but I would not build our income plan around their wages. They have their own bills.

say: **2028 thinking AI** reaches dispatch before field robots around 2031.
**Paid hands-on trials** would use the gap better than vague promises.
think: Lost **repair shifts** after 2031 could shorten my expected earning years.
Three months saved and **some local jobs** may not replace a long wage gap.
do: **Practise** paid robot stop controls on de-energised equipment if offered.
**Apply** for a posted nearby bill-covering repair job if robots cut shifts.
feel: **Anxious** about fewer paid shifts, with practical preparation possible.
S2.quote: I can learn a robot stop control, but I cannot make a second utility keep every lineworker on its rota.
fieldNote: Her **controls practice** is a new paid skill in current work, if offered.
Her **job search** becomes an application only after robot-related shift cuts and a real bill-covering vacancy.

steps.text: Practise paid robot stop controls on dead equipment if offered
Apply for posted nearby bill-covering repair job if robots cut shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years before thinking AI arrives in 2031 gives us room to test a machine in rain and wind. Field robots follow around 2034, so a safer job for an older lineworker should have a wage written beside it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be about sixty-six when capable robots arrive. Ivo and I might be ready to retire by then, but with three months saved today I cannot call it settled; I may still need the ordinary lineworker wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would review our retirement costs with Ivo every year while staying on the crew. If the employer offers paid inspection training tied to a real local job at a wage that covers bills, I would complete it before 2031 and apply during the first year after 2031; otherwise I would keep doing field repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wary, but five years is enough to compare a real offer with our bills. I would rather learn an actual line-inspection job than collect a certificate for a vacancy that never appears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make inspection training worth your time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A paid day on the actual testing equipment, a posted local role and the wage on paper. Without those, I would keep my crew shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if retirement becomes affordable first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ivo and I could choose to retire, but that would come from our own budget and wishes. I would not call the robot launch a retirement order.

say: **Wet-weather tests** should precede capable field robots that repair lines around 2034.
**Written wages** matter for a possible older-worker inspection post.
think: Retirement near **sixty-six** is possible but not funded yet.
I may still need **ordinary lineworker pay** if the budget does not work.
do: **Review** retirement costs with Ivo annually while repairing lines.
**Complete** paid inspection training only for a posted local bill-covering job.
**Apply** for that inspection job after 2031 if trained.
feel: **Wary**, but able to weigh a real offer against bills.
S3.quote: I would rather learn an actual line-inspection job than collect a certificate for a vacancy that never appears.
fieldNote: Her **training choice** depends on paid time, actual equipment, a posted local job and wages.
She leaves **retirement timing** to household costs rather than tagging a speculative early exit.

steps.text: Keep repairing lines while reviewing retirement costs with Ivo annually
Complete paid inspection training for posted local bill-covering job
Apply after 2031 if trained and posted local inspection job covers household bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade means thinking AI in 2036 and capable field robots around 2039. The original meter reading still matters when a field robot writes the power-line fault report.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be about sixty-eight at the first date, and I may have retired by then if Ivo and I can afford it. If I am still working, I would be less worried about learning new office software than about whether the line crew can stop a machine safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my repair job now and review the retirement budget with Ivo each year. In the first year after 2036, if still employed, I would help apprentices practise checking robot reports against meter sheets; if retired, I would leave the lesson to the working crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm about my own work and living. A decade is enough time for a family decision, though the numbers still have to add up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the lesson show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put a wrong switch number into a sample report and ask the apprentice to find it against the actual diagram. Nobody would touch a live line in that exercise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire early to avoid robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Ivo and I would choose a date from our budget; the 2039 robot arrival alone would not move it forward.

say: **2036 thinking AI** comes before capable physical robots repair power lines around 2039.
**Apprentices** should check robot reports against meter readings.
think: I may be **retired** before the office change if our budget allows it.
If still working, **safe stopping** matters more than another software lesson.
do: **Keep** line repair work and review retirement costs with Ivo yearly.
**Teach** robot report checks after 2036 only if still employed.
feel: **Calm** about the long runway, subject to household costs.
S4.quote: The original meter reading still matters when a field robot writes the power-line fault report.
fieldNote: She connects **apprentice teaching** to physical meter checks, not a collective campaign.
Her **retirement date** is conditional on affordability and is not brought forward for the robot schedule.

steps.text: Keep line repair work and review retirement costs with Ivo yearly

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because capable robots around 2031 could cut repair shifts before Ivo and I have enough set aside to stop working. Paid robot controls practice and a real local job with a wage that covers bills would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who tells an apprentice when the computer is wrong. I want the new lineworker to be allowed to stop a robot, even if the job order looks perfect.

portrait: **Beth Kowalski**, 58, leads an electricity line crew and holds a two-year technical diploma.
She and husband Ivo have **grown children**, ordinary pay, about three months saved and some nearby utility jobs.
She uses **AI occasionally** for handovers and will adopt a route only after a mixed field trial proves it useful.
In **AGI by 2028**, she would practise paid robot controls and seek another local wage if repair shifts shrink.
A longer **runway** lets her weigh a paid inspection post while keeping retirement tied to household costs.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut repair shifts around 2031 before her retirement finances are ready.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **robot-controls practice** would support safe work through field trials.
A real **local job** with bill-covering wages would protect income if shifts shrink.
headlineQuote: I want the new lineworker to be allowed to stop a robot, even if the job order looks perfect.
